passage:
"You got an offer from Nova Freight? That's amazing!" Abhinav said, dropping into the chair beside Deepika in the co-working space.
"Maybe. I'm checking first."
"Checking what?"
"The email came from a free mail address, not their company domain. And they want a training deposit of eight thousand, refundable."
"Refundable is fine, na?"
"Real employers don't charge you to hire you. So I looked the company up on the government company registry. It exists. Then I called the number on their official website, not the one in the email."
"And?"
"HR said they have no opening like that. Someone's using their name."
Abhinav whistled. "What about the account verification part?"
"They wanted my PAN card and to use my bank account for salary testing. No chance. Nobody uses my account or my ID."
"So now?"
"Now I report the email, and apply to their real posting."

qa.q: How much was the training deposit?
qa.a: The training deposit was eight thousand, called refundable.

qa.q: Why was Deepika cautious despite the offer?
qa.a: Deepika was suspicious because the email came from a free address and asked for a deposit, and real employers do not charge to hire.

qa.q: Which check gave Deepika the clearest answer?
qa.a: Calling the number on the company's official website, not the one in the email, revealed that HR had no such opening and someone was misusing the name.

qa.q: What would change for Abhinav after a similar email?
qa.a: Abhinav would know to check the registry, call the official number, and refuse any fee or use of a bank account, instead of assuming refundable means safe.

grounding: A person checks a job offer through official sources, refuses to pay a deposit and will not let anyone use their bank account or ID.

passage:
I'm Deepak. Last spring an agent in our town offered me a hotel job abroad, with just Rs 60,000 for processing and my passport to keep "for safety".
My cousin had gone abroad through an agent and come home with nothing, so I did three things before saying yes to anything.
First, I checked whether the agency was on the government's list of registered recruiting agents. It wasn't. Second, I wrote to the hotel through its official website. They replied that they hire only through their own careers page and never charge fees. Third, I asked my friend Gargi, who works in HR in Pune, to read the offer letter. She laughed and said, "Deepak, the logo is blurry."
I didn't pay. I didn't hand over my passport. I told the agent no and reported him to the local police.
Six months later I got a real job in Pune, through a real interview, without paying anyone a rupee.

qa.q: What did the agent want to keep for safety?
qa.a: The agent wanted to keep Deepak's passport for safety.

qa.q: Why was Deepak careful before saying yes?
qa.a: Deepak's cousin had gone abroad through an agent and come home with nothing, so Deepak felt wary and wanted proof first.

qa.q: Which of Deepak's three checks was most useful, and why?
qa.a: Writing to the hotel through its official website was decisive, because the hotel itself said it never charges fees and hires through its own careers page.

qa.q: How did Gargi see the offer letter?
qa.a: Gargi saw through it at once, noticing the blurry logo, and her outside view confirmed the doubts.

grounding: A person verifies a job offer abroad through the official agent list and the employer's own website, refuses the fee and keeps their passport.
